q-94985.name: Question 1
q-94985.problem: Which curve is defined by the equation $9{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+6{x}_{2}^{2}=10?$
q-94985.worked_solution:
Consider the quadratic form $Q(x)=9{x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+6{x}_{2}^{2}.$ To determine the curve defined by the given equation, we reduce $Q(x)$ to its canonical (diagonal) form.  

First, we write down the matrix of $Q(x),$ which is

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}9 & 2 \\ 2 & 6\end{aligned}].
$$

Next, we find the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}9-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & 6-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-15\lambda +50 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =5,\,10\end{aligned}
$$

So, our quadratic form can be reduced to $5{y}_{1}^{2}+10{y}_{2}^{2}.$ 

In the new variables, the curve has the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}5{y}_{1}^{2}+10{y}_{2}^{2} & =10 \\ \frac{{y}_{1}^{2}}{2}+\frac{{y}_{2}^{2}}{1} & =1 \\ \frac{{y}_{1}^{2}}{(\sqrt{2})^{2}}+\frac{{y}_{2}^{2}}{1} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

This is an ellipse with semiaxes $\sqrt{2}$ and $1.$

Question 1
?

Which curve is defined by the equation 9x12+4x1x2+6x22=10?

a
A hyperbola with semiaxes 1 and 2
b
An hyperbola with semiaxes 2 and 5
c
A parabola
d
A ellipse with semiaxes 2 and 1
e
A ellipse with semiaxes 2 and 1
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Consider the quadratic form Q(x)=9x12+4x1x2+6x22. To determine the curve defined by the given equation, we reduce Q(x) to its canonical (diagonal) form.

First, we write down the matrix of Q(x), which is

A=[9226].

Next, we find the eigenvalues of A:

|A−λI|=0|9−λ226−λ|=0λ2−15λ+50=0λ=5,10

So, our quadratic form can be reduced to 5y12+10y22.

In the new variables, the curve has the following equation:

5y12+10y22=10y122+y221=1y12(2)2+y221=1

This is an ellipse with semiaxes 2 and 1.

q-95002.name: Question 2
q-95002.problem: Which curve is defined by the equation $3{x}_{1}^{2}+10{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+3{x}_{2}^{2}=32?$
q-95002.worked_solution:
Consider the quadratic form $Q(x)=3{x}_{1}^{2}+10{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+3{x}_{2}^{2}.$ To determine the curve defined by the given equation, we reduce $Q(x)$ to its canonical (diagonal) form.  

First, we write down the matrix of $Q(x),$ which is

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}3 & 5 \\ 5 & 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Next, we find the eigenvalues of $A:$

$$
\begin{aligned}|A-\lambda I| & =0 \\ |\begin{aligned}3-\lambda  & 5 \\ 5 & 3-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-6\lambda -16 & =0 \\ \lambda  & =8,\,-2\end{aligned}
$$

 

So, our quadratic form can be reduced to $8{y}_{1}^{2}-2{y}_{2}^{2}.$  

In the new variables, the curve has the following equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}8{y}_{1}^{2}-2{y}_{2}^{2} & =32 \\ \frac{{y}_{1}^{2}}{4}-\frac{{y}_{2}^{2}}{16} & =1 \\ \frac{{y}_{1}^{2}}{{2}^{2}}-\frac{{y}_{2}^{2}}{{4}^{2}} & =1\end{aligned}
$$

This is a hyperbola with semiaxes  $2$ and $4.$

q-95042.name: Question 3
q-95042.problem: Find the principal axes of the curve ${x}_{1}^{2}+12{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-4{x}_{2}^{2}=40.$
q-95042.worked_solution:
First, consider the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+12{x}_{1}{x}_{2}-4{x}_{2}^{2}.$ The matrix of the form is

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 6 \\ 6 & -4\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that $A$ is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve 

$$
{x}^{T}\,Ax=40
$$

are the vectors that form an orthonormal eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

By solving the characteristic equation $|A-\lambda I|=0,$ we obtain

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=5\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=-8.$ 

Let's now find the eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-5I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 6 \\ 6 & -4\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & 6 \\ 6 & -9\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-5I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{13},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-8,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-8)1I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 6 \\ 6 & -4\end{aligned}]-(-8)[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}9 & 6 \\ 6 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-1I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{13},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\,$ $\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}3 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{13}}[\begin{aligned}-2 \\ 3\end{aligned}].$

q-95809.problem: Find the principal axes of the curve ${x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}=48.$
q-95809.worked_solution:
First, consider the quadratic form $Q(x)={x}_{1}^{2}+4{x}_{1}{x}_{2}+{x}_{2}^{2}.$ The matrix of the form is

$$
A=[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that $A$ is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve 

$$
{x}^{T}\,Ax=48
$$

are the vectors that form an orthonormal eigenvector basis of $A.$ 

By solving the characteristic equation $|A-\lambda I|=0,$ we obtain

$\,$ ${\lambda }_{1}=3\,$ and $\,{\lambda }_{2}=-1.$

Let's now find the eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=3,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-3I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]-3[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-2 & 2 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-6I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=-1,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-(-1)I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & 2 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]+1[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}2 & 2 \\ 2 & 2\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-(-1)I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{2},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\,$ $\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

q-97986.name: Question 5
q-97986.problem: Consider the matrix $A=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}]$ and the quadratic curve ${x}^{T}\,Ax=2.$ Given that $A$ has eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=5$ and ${\lambda }_{2}=0,$ find the principal axes of the curve.
q-97986.worked_solution:
Notice that $A$ is symmetric. 
The principal axes of the curve 

$$
{x}^{T}\,Ax=2
$$

are the vectors that give an orthonormal eigenvector basis for $A.$ Let's now find these eigenvectors.

- For ${\lambda }_{1}=5,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-5I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}]-5[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-4 & -2 \\ -2 & -1\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-5I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{1}=[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{1}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{1}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{1}}{‖{v}_{1}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}].
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=0,$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}A-0I & =[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}]-0[\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 0 & 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}1 & -2 \\ -2 & 4\end{aligned}].\end{aligned}
$$

Seeking a non-zero solution of $(A-0I)x=0$ gives the eigenvector ${v}_{2}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$ Dividing ${v}_{2}$ by its norm $‖{v}_{2}‖=\sqrt{5},$ we get 

$$
\frac{{v}_{2}}{‖{v}_{2}‖}=\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

$\,$ $\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}-1 \\ 2\end{aligned}]\,$ and $\,\frac{1}{\sqrt{5}}[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}].$

Question 5
?

Consider the matrix A=[1−2−24] and the quadratic curve xTAx=2. Given that A has eigenvalues λ1=5 and λ2=0, find the principal axes of the curve.

a
113[32] and 113[−23]
b
16[−511] and 16[115]
c
13[−25] and 13[52]
d
15[−12] and 15[21]
e
110[−31] and 110[13]
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Notice that A is symmetric. The principal axes of the curve

xTAx=2

are the vectors that give an orthonormal eigenvector basis for A. Let's now find these eigenvectors.

  • For λ1=5, we have A−5I=[1−2−24]−5[1001]=[−4−2−2−1]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−5I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v1=[−12]. Dividing v1 by its norm ‖v1‖=5, we get v1‖v1‖=15[−12].

  • For λ2=0, we have A−0I=[1−2−24]−0[1001]=[1−2−24]. Seeking a non-zero solution of (A−0I)x=0 gives the eigenvector v2=[21]. Dividing v2 by its norm ‖v2‖=5, we get v2‖v2‖=15[21].

Therefore, the principal axes of our curve are

15[−12] and 15[21].
